lessonTitle: Instruments and Uncertainty: Selection, Budgets and the 10-to-1 Rule

blocks.text: A shaft journal is drawn as 25.00 mm plus or minus 0.05 mm. The inspector picks up a steel rule, reads 25 mm and passes it. A second inspector measures it with a micrometer and gets 25.043. Both are 'correct' in their way, but only one instrument is fit for the job. Choosing the instrument, and knowing how much to trust its reading, is the subject of this unit.

blocks.markdown: A measurement result is never exact. It is a best estimate plus an **uncertainty**, a range within which the true value is believed to lie. Three ideas are needed: how finely an instrument can resolve, how to combine several sources of uncertainty into one number, and how much uncertainty a given tolerance can afford.

blocks.title: Resolution, accuracy and standard uncertainty
blocks.text: **Resolution** $\delta$ is the smallest change an instrument can indicate (the last digit or scale division). **Accuracy** (maximum permissible error) is the limit of error stated by the maker or calibration. A **standard uncertainty** $u$ is an uncertainty expressed as one standard deviation. If a value is only known to lie within $\pm a$ with equal likelihood (a rectangular distribution, such as rounding to the last digit), $u=a/\sqrt3$. For a resolution $\delta$ the half-width is $a=\delta/2$, so $u=\delta/(2\sqrt3)$. A calibration certificate quoting an expanded uncertainty $U$ at coverage factor $k=2$ gives $u=U/2$.

rows: General sizes, tolerances of a few tenths of a millimetre
General sizes to a tenth of a millimetre
Precision sizes to hundredths of a millimetre
Dial or digital indicator on a stand
about 0.005 mm over a short range
blocks.caption: Representative values only; always use the instrument's own specification and calibration certificate.

blocks.markdown: **Selecting by resolution.** An instrument that cannot resolve a small fraction of the tolerance cannot tell good parts from bad. The common rule is that resolution should be at most one tenth of the tolerance band $T$ (upper minus lower limit): $\delta\le T/10$. In the shaft above $T=0.10$ mm, so $\delta\le0.01$ mm; the steel rule ($0.5$ mm) and the vernier caliper ($0.02$ mm) fail, and a micrometer passes.

blocks.caption: Root-sum-of-squares combination of independent standard uncertainties u_i (all in the same unit). U is the expanded uncertainty giving about 95% coverage for a roughly normal result.

blocks.markdown: **Uncertainty budget.** List every source of error in the measurement (instrument calibration, resolution, repeatability of readings, temperature, operator and so on), convert each to a standard uncertainty, and combine them. Contributions add in quadrature because they are assumed independent; a large contribution therefore dominates, and shrinking a small one barely changes the total.

blocks.title: Uncertainty budget for a micrometer measurement
blocks.prompt: A 25 mm shaft is measured with a digital micrometer (resolution 1 micrometre). The calibration certificate gives $U=2.0\ \mu\text{m}$ ($k=2$). The standard deviation of the mean of repeated readings is $0.8\ \mu\text{m}$. The temperature may be $\pm2$ K from the reference value, the steel's expansion coefficient is $11.5\times10^{-6}\ \text{K}^{-1}$. Find the combined and expanded uncertainties.

steps.text: Calibration: divide the expanded value by $k=2$.
Repeatability: given directly as a standard deviation of the mean.
Temperature: half-width $a=25\ \text{mm}\times11.5\times10^{-6}\times2=5.75\times10^{-4}$ mm $=0.575\ \mu$m, rectangular so divide by $\sqrt3$.
Combine in quadrature, then expand with $k=2$.

blocks.answer: $u_c=1.35\ \mu$m and $U=2.7\ \mu$m. The calibration term dominates, so a better-calibrated reference would help more than a finer display.

blocks.title: The 10-to-1 rule
blocks.text: The measuring instrument's accuracy (or uncertainty) should be no more than one tenth of the tolerance band: $U_{\text{gauge}}\le T/10$. This keeps measurement error small enough that few parts are misclassified. A looser 4-to-1 ratio is sometimes accepted when 10-to-1 is impractical, at the cost of more wrong decisions near the limits.

blocks.title: Applying the 10-to-1 rule
blocks.prompt: The shaft tolerance is $\pm0.05$ mm. Is the micrometer of the previous example ($U=2.7\ \mu$m) adequate, and what if the tolerance were $\pm0.01$ mm?

steps.text: Compute the tolerance bands and allowable gauge uncertainty.

blocks.answer: For $\pm0.05$ mm the micrometer passes with a ratio of 37 to 1; for $\pm0.01$ mm the ratio is 7.4 to 1, so it falls short of 10-to-1 and a better-calibrated instrument or a comparator with a master is needed.

items: Accuracy and resolution are different: a display of 0.001 mm does not mean the reading is good to 0.001 mm.
Take readings repeatedly and use the mean; repeatability falls as $1/\sqrt{n}$.
Control temperature, or allow parts and gauges to soak, since thermal expansion of steel is about $11.5\ \mu\text{m}$ per metre per kelvin.
Report results with an uncertainty, e.g. $25.043\pm0.003$ mm ($k=2$).

blocks.title: Guard-banding
blocks.text: A part reading within 2 micrometres of a limit may really be on the wrong side. When the uncertainty is not negligible, the acceptance zone is reduced by the uncertainty at each limit (a guard band) so that accepted parts are reliably inside the tolerance.

points: Choose an instrument whose resolution, and ideally accuracy, is no more than a tenth of the tolerance band.
Convert each source to a standard uncertainty ($U/2$, $a/\sqrt3$ for rectangular), then combine in quadrature: $u_c=\sqrt{\sum u_i^2}$ and $U=2u_c$.
The 10-to-1 rule requires gauge uncertainty at most $T/10$; the dominant contributions govern the total.

questions.stem: A hole is toleranced at 12.00 mm with a total tolerance band of 0.40 mm. The inspector needs an instrument with a resolution of at most one tenth of the band. Which instrument is most appropriate?

options.text: A vernier caliper with 0.02 mm resolution
A steel rule with 0.5 mm divisions
A tape measure with 1 mm divisions
A digital micrometer with 0.001 mm resolution, because finer is always better

questions.correctOptionText: A vernier caliper with 0.02 mm resolution

distractorRationale.a: The required resolution is $0.40/10=0.04$ mm and the 0.02 mm vernier caliper meets it.
distractorRationale.b: 0.5 mm is larger than the whole 0.40 mm tolerance band, so it cannot resolve good from bad.
distractorRationale.c: This is even coarser than the steel rule and unsuited to this tolerance.
distractorRationale.d: It meets the requirement but is slower and costlier than the task needs; the question asks for the appropriate instrument.

questions.explanation: The rule $\delta\le T/10$ sets the limit at 0.04 mm. The vernier caliper satisfies it with margin, whereas the rule and tape cannot resolve the band and a micrometer is unnecessary.

questions.stem: A digital caliper shows 25.43 mm and resolves to 0.01 mm. Considering only the display resolution, within what range does the value lie?

options.text: $25.43\pm0.005$ mm, since the last digit rounds to the nearest 0.01 mm
$25.43\pm0.01$ mm, the full resolution on each side
Exactly 25.43 mm, since digital instruments have no resolution error
$25.43\pm0.05$ mm, a tenth of the display

questions.correctOptionText: $25.43\pm0.005$ mm, since the last digit rounds to the nearest 0.01 mm

distractorRationale.a: Rounding to the nearest 0.01 mm leaves a half-width of 0.005 mm.
distractorRationale.b: The rounding error is half a step either way, not a full step.
distractorRationale.c: Resolution limits what is displayed; the true value can differ from the display.
distractorRationale.d: A tenth of the display is not a rounding limit.

questions.explanation: A reading displayed to a step $\delta$ corresponds to a true value within $\pm\delta/2$. This is only the display's contribution and is added to calibration and repeatability uncertainties.

questions.stem: An uncertainty budget has two independent contributions: 10 micrometres and 1 micrometre. What is the combined standard uncertainty, and what does this show?

options.text: 11 micrometres, because uncertainties are added directly
5.5 micrometres, because they are averaged
About 7.1 micrometres, the geometric mean
About 10.05 micrometres, which shows that the small contribution is practically irrelevant

questions.correctOptionText: About 10.05 micrometres, which shows that the small contribution is practically irrelevant

distractorRationale.a: Independent contributions combine in quadrature, not by direct addition.
distractorRationale.b: The combined uncertainty is not an average.
distractorRationale.c: There is no geometric-mean rule in uncertainty combination.

questions.explanation: In quadrature, squares add, so a small contribution adds almost nothing to a large one. This is why effort goes into reducing the dominant term rather than the small ones.

questions.stem: A gauge has an accuracy of 0.004 mm. Using the 10-to-1 rule, what is the smallest total tolerance band it can be used to inspect?

options.text: 0.4 mm

distractorRationale.a: This would give a 1-to-1 ratio, the gauge error equal to the whole tolerance.
distractorRationale.d: This satisfies the rule but is not the smallest band it can inspect.

questions.explanation: The rule says gauge accuracy should be at most a tenth of the tolerance band, so the band must be at least ten times the accuracy. A smaller band would leave the gauge error too large a share of it.

questions.stem: A calibration certificate states an expanded uncertainty of 3.0 micrometres at $k=2$ for a gauge block. What standard uncertainty should be used in the budget, and why?

options.text: 3.0 micrometres, because certificates quote standard uncertainty
6.0 micrometres, because the budget uses expanded uncertainty doubled
1.5 micrometres, because the expanded value must be divided by the coverage factor
0.87 micrometres, by dividing by $\sqrt{12}$

questions.correctOptionText: 1.5 micrometres, because the expanded value must be divided by the coverage factor

distractorRationale.a: Certificates normally quote the expanded uncertainty with its coverage factor.
distractorRationale.b: Multiplying again would overstate the uncertainty.
distractorRationale.d: That conversion applies to a resolution step, not to a quoted expanded uncertainty.

questions.explanation: The budget combines standard uncertainties, each equal to one standard deviation. An expanded uncertainty at $k=2$ is two standard deviations, so it must be halved before combining.

questions.stem: Three independent standard uncertainties in a measurement are 3 micrometres (calibration), 4 micrometres (repeatability) and 12 micrometres (temperature). Calculate the combined standard uncertainty in micrometres.
questions.explanation: Combine in quadrature: $\sqrt{3^2+4^2+12^2}=\sqrt{9+16+144}=\sqrt{169}=13$ micrometres. The temperature term dominates the result.

questions.stem: A digital gauge displays to a resolution of 0.005 mm. Treating the rounding as a rectangular distribution, calculate the standard uncertainty due to resolution in micrometres.
questions.explanation: The half-width is $\delta/2=0.0025$ mm, and the standard uncertainty is $\delta/(2\sqrt3)=0.005/3.464=0.001443$ mm. That is 1.44 micrometres.

questions.stem: A bore has a tolerance of $\pm0.025$ mm. Using the 10-to-1 rule on the total tolerance band, what is the largest permitted gauge accuracy (uncertainty) in micrometres?
questions.explanation: The tolerance band is $2\times0.025=0.050$ mm, so $T/10=0.005$ mm. This is 5.0 micrometres.

questions.stem: Three features on a part have total tolerance bands of 0.50 mm, 0.06 mm and 0.012 mm. Using the 10-to-1 rule for resolution and accuracy, state the required resolution and accuracy for each, and recommend (with reasons) a suitable class of instrument from the typical values in the lesson table.
markingGuide: 0.50 mm: needs 0.05 mm, so a vernier or digital caliper suffices
0.06 mm: needs 0.006 mm; caliper (0.01 to 0.02 mm) is not good enough, a micrometer is appropriate (resolution 0.001 mm, accuracy about 0.004 mm)
0.012 mm: needs 0.0012 mm; a micrometer is marginal, needs a high-accuracy comparator or CMM with calibration
Justification links tolerance to instrument capability
questions.explanation: The 10-to-1 rule gives required values of 0.05 mm, 0.006 mm and 0.0012 mm. The first is met by a caliper, the second needs a micrometer, and the third demands a more accurate comparator because even a good micrometer is marginal.

questions.stem: A measurement of a shaft length uses a gauge with the following contributions: calibration certificate $U=1.6$ micrometres at $k=2$, resolution 2 micrometres, repeatability (standard deviation of the mean) 1.2 micrometres, and a temperature effect of half-width 1.5 micrometres (rectangular). Build the uncertainty budget, find $u_c$ and $U$ with $k=2$, and state whether the 10-to-1 rule is met for a tolerance of $\pm0.02$ mm.
markingGuide: Repeatability $u=1.2$ micrometres (given as standard deviation of the mean)
Tolerance band 40 micrometres; $T/10=4$ micrometres; $3.56<4$ so the rule is met (ratio about 11 to 1)
questions.explanation: Converting each term to a standard uncertainty and combining in quadrature gives $u_c=1.78$ micrometres and $U=3.56$ micrometres. The tolerance band is 40 micrometres, so the allowable gauge uncertainty is 4 micrometres and the rule is satisfied with a ratio of about 11 to 1.
